Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington. The paramount British military figure of the Napoleonic Wars, defeating French forces across Europe and finally Napoleon himself at Waterloo.

Wellington earned the title the Iron Duke for his disciplined tactics and relentless pursuit of French armies in the Peninsula War from 1808 to 1814. These campaigns established him as Britain's greatest field commander. He defeated Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815 alongside Prussian allies, ending the Emperor's Hundred Days and cementing Britain's role as the guarantor of European order.

Though Wellington's tenure as Prime Minister from 1828 to 1830 was brief and unpopular, his military legacy dominated British national consciousness for decades. As PM, he reluctantly supported Catholic emancipation in 1829, recognizing that denial risked Irish rebellion. The move alienated his Tory base and hastened his departure from office.

Wellington was deeply unpopular as a peacetime Prime Minister, seen as an aristocratic relic out of step with reform. His government fell in 1830 over the refusal to extend the franchise to new voters, signaling his inability to adapt to the political currents of a changing age. Yet he remained a towering figure in British life, repeatedly called upon for public service and revered as the embodiment of martial virtue and national defense. He died in 1852 and received a state funeral of unparalleled splendor.
